posts.title: Corruption Taking Lives
posts.excerpt: Corruption is usually judged as a pecuniary undue advantage, but this article traces how it sits behind rampant industrial accidents that end up taking thousands of lives.
posts.body:
*Case Laws are ten percent law and ninety percent story*

> “A survey came to the conclusion that even among the educated classes 97 percent of the people could not think for themselves. They derived their opinions and beliefs from what they heard on the radio or television or read in the newspapers.” - Nani Palkhivala

Sutherland must not have anticipated a blood splattered white shirt inside a blue blazer or else he would not have given the name "White" Collar Crime. Traditionally, violence and White Collar Crime were considered mutually exclusive and it was not until the turn of the century that this notion became antiquated. Similarly, the author believes that Corruption, which is largely judged as a pecuniary undue advantage, is capable of much more. On a macro level, corruption can be seen as a multi-faceted crime with it being able to range from a small harmless bribe to a deadly destruction of a bridge. However, this article would try to tell how corruption is behind the occurrence of rampant Industrial accidents which end up taking thousands of lives.

### Industrial Accidents

**Uphaar Tragedy:** One of the most heart-wrenching and deadly incident is the Uphaar theatre fire breakout case wherein a short-circuit in the transformer situated inside the premises of the theatre. Soon the toxic gases spread into the hall and choked the spectators. It sounds like an accident but further investigations showed blatant violations of safety norms, for instance, there was only one exit for 300-panic stricken people.

**Vizag Gas Leak:** A replication of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy case, this gas leak happened due to the Auto-Polymerisation reaction that occurs when Styrene is stored for a long time in liquid form in stagnancy. Sources state that the necessary temperature check was absent which could have been controlled if there were adequate staff present. Moreover, the plant was using a huge percentage of contractual workers instead of permanent staff.

**Sattarghat Bridge Collapse:** This particular bridge collapse put the Kolkata state government and other administration department in the dock for a bridge was constructed in a densely populated part of the town by a company which went bankrupt two years before being assigned with the tender. 21 people died and hundreds injured because of the corrupt intent of the authorities.

The habit of making money by using low quality material and giving tenders to the lowest bidder but not the best bidder seems like a commonality these days. Businessmen violate norms and standards, employ less skilled worker for highly skilled jobs and abuse the rule of law for more profit making and unfortunately the public officials let them.

However, what is more catastrophic for the nation and its citizens is not just conventionally understood corruption where a public official violates norms of public office for selfish reasons. It is the soft corruption wherein violation by public official happens within the legal purview wherein both the public official and the private player leave with brimming pockets.

Private sector corruption is very rampant but it is the public level corruption which has massive impact, socially and economically, on the society. One of the biggest flaws of Indian government has been its inability to enforce Procurement reforms which can prove to be a step towards greater transparency in the nation.

### The Attempt At Reforming Public Procurement

In 2012, the Public Procurement Bill was sought to be enacted with the objectives transparency, fair and equitable treatment of bidders, promote competition and enhance efficiency and economy in the procurement process. This was a step forward in India, considering that different departments/ministries had their own procedures to supplement General Financial Rules, 2005. Unfortunately, the bill never saw the light of the day and such an important legislation is still hanging in the wardrobe of our Parliament.

Currently, three states have public procurement bill, the most recent one being Punjab's Transparency in Public Procurement Act, 2019. As interesting as the concept of 'debarment' and 'blacklisting' may sound, the Punjab legislation has not even defined these phrases. Rajasthan and Assam are the other two states which have procurement laws, both of which have been copy-pasted from UNCITRAL model.

### Models for establishing sustainable anti-corruption reform

But it all boils down to the model solution, right? As in what is the model plan to fight corruption? The following four points sum up the methodologies suggested and followed worldwide for ensuring a sustainable anti-corruption model;

**Model 1 – ONE LEADER ARMY:** Herein, there is a charismatic leader and people have faith in the leader's anti-corrupt motives which leads to fewer checks on his authority. Although Singapore has followed this model quite successfully, it does come with its own reservations and riders.

**Model 2 – BREAKAGE IN THE STATUS QUO:** Experts envisage that waiting for a disruption in political status quo can act as an opportunity to bring in political reforms which would otherwise be too difficult to do. Indonesia's New Order can be a good example of it.

**Model 3 – INDIRECT REFORMS:** If reformers are smart enough to bring in reforms in a manner that the current regime doesn't feel threatened by it then maybe a sustainable model can be built.

**Model 4 – CIVIL SOCIETY:** Experts state that civil society, which includes educational institutions, parents, religious institutions amongst other things, can play an immensely important role in bringing long-term anti-corruption reforms.

### Conclusions

Regarding the unfortunate Beirut Blast, the OCCPR reports suggested that the Lebanese government's disposal of public duties, which ought to be performed by public functionaries, had major deficiencies. The report hinted towards involvement of corruption.

Yury Fedotov once said, “Corruption is the thief of economic and social development; stealing the opportunities of ordinary people to progress and to prosper”, I believe that corruption can be more than a thief. From a small street pick pocket to a mass murderer, a corrupt act can put on stake lives of thousands. Law plays an irreplaceable role in keeping the checks and balances intact but those legal pillars are not immune from cracks and crevices. That is where the role of Civil Society comes into picture. When trust in government's fight against corruption is declining, it is imperative to make space for civil societies to play more of a role.

posts.title: Whose Delhi Is It Anyway? Constitutional Bench Judgement
posts.excerpt: The conflict between Delhi's Lieutenant Governor and elected representatives resulted in a 5-judge constitutional bench ruling in Govt. of NCT vs. Union of India.
posts.body:
The conflict between Delhi's Lieutenant Governor and elected representatives resulted in a 5-judge constitutional bench ruling in *Govt. of NCT vs. Union of India*. The judgment addressed three key questions:

1. Status of Delhi under the Constitution  
2. Lieutenant Governor and Council of Ministers' legislative and executive relationship under Article 239AA  
3. Can the LG refer “every matter” to the President?

Three of the five judges issued separate concurring opinions, each examining these issues through different legal frameworks.

### CJI D. Misra's Opinion

Justice Misra relied on precedent from *NDMC v. State of Punjab*, establishing that Delhi cannot become a state. However, he determined that Article 239AA created a hybrid arrangement distinct from typical Union Territories.

Writing with Justices Sikri and Khanwilkar, Misra characterized the Lt. Governor as “an administrator in a limited sense” separate from a state governor. He noted that Article 239AA embeds the principle of Collective Responsibility: the Council of Ministers must answer to the Delhi Legislature, similar to how Union Ministers answer to Lok Sabha under Article 74.

Misra concluded that treating the LG as executive head would undermine representative government and defeat the 69th Amendment's purpose. He also stated: “the phrase 'every matter' cannot be interpreted as 'any matter'.”

### Justice Ashok Bhushan's Opinion

Justice Bhushan asserted Delhi cannot be considered a State, noting the 69th Amendment created neither a full legislature nor state status. While agreeing the LG lacks final executive authority over the Council of Ministers, he invoked Section 49 of The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991, positioning both entities as subordinate to the President.

He clarified that “every matter” cannot mean “any matter” and that LG concurrence is unnecessary regarding matters where Delhi's elected government has clear legislative and executive powers.

### Justice D.Y. Chandrachud's Opinion

Justice Chandrachud agreed Delhi is not a state but argued Article 239AA's intent was creating “representative government” for the territory. Delhi cannot operate like other Union Territories under direct gubernatorial control; the 69th Amendment established a cabinet system.

He noted that only matters of “vital national interests” may be reserved for Presidential reference. Even then, the LG must follow the three-step Transaction of Business Rules, 1993: attempt resolution with the minister, then with the Council of Ministers, and only as a final recourse contact the President.

### Conclusion

This judgment's strength lies in its varied judicial reasoning and application of different legal principles. Justice Bhushan's approach appears more literal and strict, granting greater Presidential authority. Justice Chandrachud's opinion constrains the LG to referring only restricted matters through prescribed procedures.

The ruling establishes that popular government must remain accountable to its people, and accountability requires adequate authority.

posts.title: Whose Delhi is it anyway?
posts.excerpt: As a resident or stakeholder of Delhi, you might want to know how much power your elected representative actually holds, right?
posts.body:
After reading for quite a while about Delhi and its affairs, one thing seems sorted. And it is the fact that Delhi is at its peak (no! not the three garbage mountains guarding Delhi's periphery) of harmony and development whenever the Center and Delhi's political alignment flow in the same direction. Well, this might seem to be the case with every state and center relationship but a capital is different from a routine state (also, Delhi is a Union territory). And so a central government has a special focus on the capital. However, as a resident or stakeholder of Delhi, you might want to know how much power your elected representative holds, right?

Let me illustrate one scenario. You live in a country named X. Every citizen of X has a right to representation among many other civil liberties. You, however, live in a "special" city where you pay all the taxes which you assume fellow citizens of other states must also be paying. Your family and friends have been into wars just like many others. You do have a representative who can make laws for your specific needs but she doesn't get to vote in the Big House. That is, she as your candidate can look at the beauty that law making is but her agreement to it won't ever matter. And hence, yours too. The territory you live in cannot be called a state and because it is special it does not form part of Central policy. So, any incentives or packages that the other citizens of X got as part of Federal policy will not be received by you. Do you blame the contours of your territory or the big fat book which swore for equality and basic rights?

Well, this is not a case Indians will be familiar with but the residents of Washington D.C. might find it relatable. Fortunately, the people and their elected representative of Delhi do not have to go through such a humiliation yet one is coerced to look into the nuances of what is Delhi's and what is not.

The answer is not so simple. It does not merely lie in the fact that the Government of NCT Delhi is specifically excluded from legislative or executive power with respect to Entry 1 (Public Order), Entry 2 (Police) and Entry 18 (Land) of List II and Entries 64, 65 and 66 of that List insofar as they relate to the said Entries 1, 2 and 18. [Read Article 239AA].

I can say it because in the year 2017 six civil appeals were filed by five different (eminent, I must say) lawyers on issues which the GNCTD (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) thought and claimed they had executive powers over. All these appeals were decided by a three-judge bench in 2019 post the CB judgement on the status of Delhi, inter alia. The full bench judgement relies heavily on the CB decision and so in the next post I will summarize the latter judgement in order to ease ourselves when we discuss the six appeals in excruciating detail.

---

**Comment - min (7 Oct 2020):** “looking forward to your next post”

posts.title: Saving Dissent by Dissent: Bhima Koregaon Case
posts.excerpt: Justice Chandrachud's dissent, carved out on facts and evidence rather than pure law, has paved the way for a more liberal interpretation of Article 32.
posts.body:
“It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen”, the opening line of the novel *1984*. The chills I get, the weirdness that envelopes my mind, and that too every single time, is uncanny. But why am I mentioning this? We are not living in an Orwellian era. Right?

Cut to Hecuba (people were questioning my promises of brevity), *Romila Thapar & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.*, 2018, is a case filed by Ms. Romilla Thapar and others on behalf of five human rights activists who were arrested for a crime they probably didn't commit. But before deliberating on the judgement, it is pertinent to give a background as this forms the core of this judgement.

### Background

Bhima Koregaon is the name of the battle which took place between the East India Company and Peshwa Baji Rao II in Koregaon, Maharashtra. The reason for the battle was that Baji Rao II did not want to cede to the East India Company's agreement which cut down their revenue and other lordship privileges. And Baji Rao II was reluctant to do so. Dalit soldiers also constituted the East India Army. And the Marathas lost that battle.

Mahars (who have unfortunately been considered as the 'untouchables' by society back then) celebrate this victory of the East India Company as a mark of the end of the high-caste Brahmins who oppressed and insulted them. Consequently, an obelisk was erected as a memory of the soldiers who died battling the Peshwas. An annual event is conducted at the Battle Site to celebrate Dalit Rights and even B.R. Ambedkar visited it in 1927 to mark its 101st anniversary.

After centuries of celebration of that event, violence happened for the first time in 2018. What the specific reason for the uprising was is unclear, but organizations like Akhil Bhartiya Brahamin Mahasabha, Rashtriya Ekatmata, Rashtriya Abhiyan, Hindu Aghadi criticised the event by stating that Mahars fought even in the Peshwa army and added “what are they celebrating? Victory of British over Marathas?”

### Issue of the Instant Case

The primary complaint was registered on 2nd January, 2018 (yes, dates are vital) against the Elgar Parishad held at Shaniwar Wada where (as mentioned in the FIR) Sagar Gokhale, Sudhir Dhavale, Jyoti Jagtap, Ramesh Gaychor, *inter alia*, were present at the Parishad. Elgar Parishad was held on 31st December, 2017 and the Bhima Koregaon celebration is celebrated every year on 1st January. The FIR reported that at the Elgar Parishad there were continuous communal and violent chants, stone pelting and arson.

A second and fake FIR was filed on 8th January, 2018 where five well-known human rights activists, who claim they were not even present at the site, let alone inciting anything, were eventually arrested on the ground of inciting communal violence. Pune Police, AFTER conducting raids on their houses, which were NOT located in one city or even one state, found incriminating material like links with CPI (Maoist), a banned organisation. Interestingly, the first FIR which named Sagar Gokhale led to neither an arrest nor an investigation.

But this is not what hit Justice Chandrachud.

### The Dissent

I feel it is pertinent to mention that Justice Chandrachud dissented this judgement, as he mentions, on “principle”.

His dissent revolved around the 'fairness' with which the Police approached the investigation. On 29th September, 2018, the Joint Commissioner of Pune Police held a press conference claiming they had found more than sufficient evidence (like letters to assassinate the Prime Minister) whose remand order had been stayed by the court. The video was uploaded to a social media forum, within hours of the Court's order, on unverified facts and evidence. The purpose was to influence public opinion and create pressure on the judiciary. Justice Chandrachud called it a “disconcerted” behaviour.

Justice Chandrachud dissected a letter found allegedly at Ms. Sudha Bhardwaj's (one of the activists under house arrest) house. The following was observed by the Justice regarding that one letter;

a) it was an undated letter  
b) there was no letterhead  
c) Sudha Bhardwaj, who is not of Marathi descent and has never lived in Maharashtra, could not have possibly written a letter in Marathi grammar.

Another controversial aspect of the investigation was that the Police had not followed Section 41-B of the CrPC which deals with the independence of witnesses while making an arrest. That is, two employees of the Pune Municipal Corporation were made witnesses and they travelled as part of the Police team. This is not just a violation of the Code but also of the law laid down in the landmark judgement of DK Basu.

These facts cast aspersions on the modus operandi adopted by the Police. And the fact that the human rights activists were arrested on these grey allegations, and that there was even an attempt to taint their case through electronic media, could not be swallowed by the dissenting judge.

The petitioners (not the accused human rights activists) had filed this petition demanding an independent probe into the matter by setting up an SIT so as to ensure an independent investigation. The majority, comprising Justice Khanwilkar and Chief Justice Dipak Misra, had reasoned that the accused does not have a right to choose their investigating agency.

Justice Chandrachud, however, disagreed and said that the Court had wide powers under Article 32. He used precedents to support the position that in situations where the investigation itself appears unfair, the Supreme Court can order an independent investigation for the accused. Because nothing is more important than a fair chance. Interestingly, one of the judgements cited in his dissent was that of Justice Khanwilkar himself. In Justice Khanwilkar's judgement in *E. Sivakumar v. Union of India*, the following had been held by his lordship,

> “It is the bounden duty of a court of law to uphold the truth and truth means absence of deceit, absence of fraud and in a criminal investigation a real and fair investigation, not an investigation that reveals itself as a sham one.”

### Conclusion

Although Justice D.Y. Chandrachud is known for penning many dissents, I was particularly intrigued by this one. The primary reason being that the dissent is carved out on the facts and evidence of the case, not on hardcore points of law. The dissent has paved the way for a more liberal interpretation of Article 32, whose scope has been rightly expanded by the learned judge. The actual importance of this dissent lies in the entangling web of right-wing oriented politics against which not many judges speak. The executive authorities use media to put blinders on ordinary people's peripheral vision. Justice Chandrachud, through his wisdom and dissent, has impacted this domain as well.

Unfortunately, people outside the legal domain would rarely get to know about this revelation.

posts.title: What's in an Internet Connection? Part II
posts.excerpt: The real problem with the Anuradha Bhasin judgement wasn't entirely the judgement. It was the 5-month hiatus that the people of Kashmir had to endure.
posts.body:
The flowery meadows, a frozen river and falling apples: your land is no less than heaven. Born and brought up in this heavenly abode, you feel embers converting into a volcano whenever it is painted red by assailants. But as fate is, you cannot really do anything except record the echo of those bombs in your diary.

However this time the situation is a bit different. Some local people of your society are upset over something the previous governments have not even dared to touch. Actually, they are more than upset. Thankfully, only over social media. But if provoked more, they can come to the streets, and if they also start carrying those burning bottles as trophies, would you loathe them as you do terrorists? “Oh god,” you pray, “can you stop this internet just for a second?”

If this narrative failed in providing another aspect to the case, then the government's submissions might.

41,886. This is the count of total **lives lost** due to militant activity since 1990, cross border and otherwise. Out of this, 14,038 are **civilians** and 5,929 **military personnel**. (See how impactful numbers are.) The government went on to submit a series of inciting speeches and tweets available in the public domain. One of the tweets made by Ms. Mehbooba Mufti has been reproduced as follows;

> “Don't play with fire; don't fiddle with Article-35A, else you will see what you haven't seen since 1947, if it's attacked then I don't know which flag people of J&K will be forced to pick up instead of the tricolour.”

The government further submitted that many separatists tried provoking Kashmiris through tweets and speeches. One of them, also submitted by the party, was;

> “YES! need MASSIVE protests against India's escalation in #Kashmir! Talk to friends. Set a date. Take to the streets of #London #Paris #Istanbul #Islamabad & #Copenhagen. One loud unison NO to this escalation/attack on Kashmir! #India #Pakistan #KashmirUnderThreat”

The respondent, hence, used these types of evidence to justify the government's act of enforcing Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In effect, the apex court agreed with the government's imposition of the curfew and also partially assented to the internet shutdown in the Valley, stating that it was necessary to curb the imminent danger and the potential loss of life. The point, however, which pinched everybody was that the Court did not deal with the government with a heavy hand and instead ordered a weekly review by a committee set up under the Temporary Suspension of Telecom Services Rules, 2017. Surely, the court did reprimand the government for not passing a public order for the imposition of such a strict curfew.

But the real problem with the *Anuradha Bhasin* judgement wasn't entirely the judgement. It was the 5-month hiatus that the people of Kashmir had to face because of the lethargic process of the Court, which resulted in an unabated internet shutdown in the region.

Keeping aside these inhibitions (I will take them up in another post, don't worry), let's focus on the Anuradha Bhasin case for this post. As I mentioned previously, the approach adopted by the petitioner was, to some extent, based on anecdotal evidence, and the respondent's approach was to give facts and figures in the courtroom. This divide reminds me of the great Aswath Damodaran who, through his book *Numbers and Narratives*, explained how important it is to give a story to your numbers. He explains that a story without a number is almost always unconvincing, and a number without a story attaches no value to the human mind. Where the petitioner relied too much on story, the respondent did not just give facts and figures but attached a story, a background to it which, fortunately or unfortunately, provided more weight to their arguments.

Before I sign off, I want you to weigh this in your own manner. There is absolutely no replacement for the hardship suffered by Kashmiris due to the unavailability of internet for months altogether. However, if someone threatens a person with impending actions, then even he or she would upgrade their locks, right?

posts.title: What's in an Internet Connection?
posts.excerpt: The petition filed by Anuradha Bhasin against the sudden imposition of curfew in the newly created UT of Jammu and Kashmir explains the internet shutdown in the Valley.
